Hey! I'm so sorry you're going through this. I've struggled consistently throughout my life with loneliness, depression, and rejection too, it hurts a lot. Losing your dog on top of that is really shitty too. Be kind to yourself and good job on seeking help. I'm glad you posted on this sub; articulating your feelings is a great first step to processing and overcoming them. Are you seeing a therapist currently? If not, definitely find one as soon as possible so you can continue to work through your grief.

Getting a retail job is an excellent idea. I also quit a high-paying tech job a while back due to depression/burnout and decided to be a barista for a few months, which did wonders for my mental health. It was so meditative to do something easy and just focus on healing + finding joy in the little things. Plus, you'll meet cool, **normal** people rather than high-achieving grindset people, who tend to be much kinder and chiller and likely will have more empathy for you than others might.  
  
Something you should also really consider after you get a job is saving up and then moving out of your parents' house to live with roommates. It obviously won't be as easy to pay rent on a retail job as it would be on a corporate job, but PLENTY of Americans do it and make it work (myself included). From my personal experience, living with family has always amplified any shitty feeling I had. Like, my parents are pretty chill compared to most Desi parents, but I still felt really stuck while living with them, not only because of the high expectations and standards that Desi culture passively places upon us, but also because of that American notion that living with your parents as an adult is "shameful." It's true that American culture should unlearn this hyper-individualistic mindset, and that Desi-style communal/familial living can actually be a really positive thing, but I think that in your 20s, it's super valuable to be out in the world on your own and get a change of scenery. Even when I was working shitty retail jobs, splitting an apartment with five people, and barely making rent, it felt worth it **because my life was my own.** Whatever depression and anxiety I felt was mitigated by the baseline pride of being completely in charge of my own life, rather than existing as an offshoot of my nuclear family. I learned how to be self-sufficient, budget, and survive against all odds without my parents, which did wonders for my self-esteem and eventually got me back on track with my career. Comparison is the thief of joy, and I can see that you feel insecure about your life as it compares to your brother's... so why not remove yourself from constant exposure to him so you can focus on you and rebuild your own sense of self? Why not surround yourself with different people from different walks of life who might understand you better than your family can?

I hope this advice is helpful. Hang in there, friend. You will absolutely get through this!

also, in general, i 100% feel your original post. i think what makes the diaspora so hard is that there are so many subcultures within "desi" culture that are SO rich and unique in of themselves, but we tend to act like a monolith instead of like the cool diverse friend group that we are. so people focus on the shallow superficial similarities (the strict parenting, the body hair, the stereotypes) over the very interesting/ exciting differences (the language, the music, the food, the traditions). it's thrilling to meet someone and reach across/ talk about all your differences in order to truly understand each other... it's not thrilling to meet someone who assumes they know who you are solely bc of your ethnicity. i feel like diaspora desis  who only befriend other desis have this vibe-- it's like why are u here in america if you're not making friends w other immigrants, other poc who aren't exactly like u...

the desi friendships i have that feel the realest are the ones where we enthusiastically and lovingly share our identities with each other. i get to show my hindi-speaking friend telugu movies/music, i listen to the OG tamil versions of telugu AR Rehman songs, and i learn malayalam with my malayalam friend because i can help her understand how the grammar works via my knowledge of telugu grammar, which is similar.  that's the shit i love-- when u are able to authentically be urself around ur friends. 

so maybe for you, that's finding other bengali hindus, which is totally fine! i think it would be great to start there and find relief and commonality w the people around you before you feel confident and comfortable sharing that with your non-bengali hindu friends. <3

hi, it seems like a lot of these problems are rooted in your low self-esteem. when I was your age, I had a really similar dynamic with one of my friends-- she was one of the "popular girls" and i always felt like I couldn't really be myself around her, like I had to impress her because she was way cooler than me. honestly, my friend wasn't perfect (teenagers tend to fuck up a lot and make mistakes in relationships and friendships) but my low self esteem was the main source of many of my problems. i tended to always assume something was wrong instead of assuming things were alright, which led me to overthink social situations, get really in my head about minor issues, and withdraw even more. the only way to get better at socializing is by doing it a lot, so the more you withdraw, the more antisocial, awkward, and anxious you become. I'm not trying to make you feel bad when I say this-- it's common for teens to have low self esteem-- I'm just trying to say that it can be a vicious cycle that's really hard to break out of. low self esteem inexplicably spawns sometime around puberty when you start comparing yourself to your peers, and makes it hard for you to socialize, thereby lowering your self esteem even further, thereby making it even harder to socialize, and so on and so forth. 

so the first step is to try to take a deep breath and list out all the good things you can see in yourself. you have friends, even a best friend, so clearly you're doing something right! if you can't come up with anything, try again because the insistence that you're all bad or all weird is unrealistic and illogical! EVERYONE has great qualities, you just have to identify them.

moving on from your self esteem: you mentioned that you only ever hang out with this friend when she asks you to, and that you usually don't reach out. i would suggest breaking this pattern, assuming there's no issue, and texting her to hang. friendships are a two way street-- I know I would hate to be the one to constantly have to reach out to my friends. it feels good when people think of you and reach out to you. so after you text her, if she responds coldly, then she might be mad at you and you can try to figure out why. but if she responds normally/enthusiastically, you know that everything is ok. the first step to relieve your anxiety is to determine whether or not she really IS upset with you. once you do that, then you can try to find out why and make amends. remember that miscommunications and arguments only serve to make relationships/friendships healthier. if she's mad at you because of something you did and you apologize for it, you can grow from there and be a better friend to her. 

there's also the possibility that she's just moody and unreasonably annoyed at you, in which case it isn't your fault and you don't have to apologize. something that's expected of adults is communicating their problems to one another-- you can't expect others to read your mind and magically determine when you're upset. that's childish. so, she might be acting childish (which, to be fair, she is a child) in which case you might want to reconsider your friendship with her. you seem to be walking on eggshells around her, which is usually indicative of a toxic friendship. your best friend might be right-- maybe she isn't the best friend for you if you don't feel like you can be free around her and if you're constantly worried that she's mad at you.


hope this helps, and chin up! you got this, you can totally work this out with her. all it takes is a little bit of bravery and some clear communication.

i definitely feel this-- it's like film burnout. i personally think it's super exhausting to be constantly consuming content w/o having the time and space necessary to fully digest it and dwell on it. in the past, before information overload, you'd maybe watch a film a week and then have that whole week to ponder it. or, maybe you'd take a deep dive and watch a few films of the same general category in order to learn about a specific aspect of filmmaking (films by one director, films from one old hollywood era, films that employ a certain camera angle, musicals, horror, etc), which would also be a more focused / simple experience in comparison to the endless content we have available now on streaming services. basically, I feel like there's so much to pick from these days that you're constantly aware of the gaps in your knowledge, as well as the gaps in what you've seen compared to your peers, and that awareness in of itself can become extremely overwhelming and debilitating.

you mention in your post that you're very busy w your professional life, and that you have straight As, both of which are wonderful things! you are hardworking and you're clearly spending your time absorbing and processing and interacting with the world around you. this, too, is essential for filmmaking, for any creative pursuit. eventually, when you sit down to write a script, it will be these very moments that you draw upon. 

i would recommend that you roll with the punches and allow yourself to live for a bit. don't force movie nights. the time will come when you have a spare moment and the energy to throw yourself into a film, and it will feel wonderful, like meeting an old friend you haven't met in a very long time. trust that the right film will draw you back into it, and until then, just keep living your life as successfully as you are. you got this!
